name: Fenfluramine / phentermine (Fen-Phen)

lead: Fen-phen was the nickname for taking fenfluramine and phentermine together to lose weight in the 1990s. It was used to cut appetite, shed weight and get leaner.

Fenfluramine mainly releases serotonin and phentermine mainly releases norepinephrine, and together they suppress appetite. A 1984 trial reported greater weight loss than placebo, and use grew widely through the 1990s.

paras: It was prescribed as a two-drug combination for weight loss. It is no longer available, and it is cited today as a historical diet-drug example and as the reason later serotonergic obesity drugs were screened for valve safety.

In 1997 reports of heart valve abnormalities led the FDA to request withdrawal of fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine, and the episode produced tens of thousands of lawsuits. Documented harms are valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension, attributed to fenfluramine's activation of 5-HT2B receptors on heart valves.

angle.text: Fen-phen paired two appetite suppressants that act on serotonin and norepinephrine, so people ate less and lost weight. It produced weight loss in its era and was withdrawn in 1997 after heart valve problems.

lead: Fen-phen is the informal name for the combination of the appetite suppressants fenfluramine and phentermine, which was prescribed for weight loss in the United States in the 1990s. [1] Fenfluramine mainly releases serotonin, while phentermine mainly releases norepinephrine. [1]

The combination grew popular after a 1984 trial by University of Rochester researchers reported greater weight loss than placebo. [1] In 1997 a Mayo Clinic report linked it to heart valve abnormalities, and the FDA requested withdrawal of fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine in September 1997. [1] The episode produced tens of thousands of lawsuits. [1]

No looksmaxxing-community material about fen-phen was identified. It is documented here as a historical weight-loss drug combination, and as the reason later serotonergic obesity drugs were screened for valve safety.

paras: The combination was prescribed to treat obesity, usually as a long-term regimen. National survey data from the period describe a large rise in prescription of antiobesity medications in the 1990s. [2][3]

Fenfluramine alone was introduced in the 1970s and sold modestly because its weight loss was temporary. A 1984 double-blind trial from the University of Rochester reported about 8.4 kg lost over 24 weeks with the combination versus 4.4 kg with placebo, with fewer side effects than either drug alone. [1]
A later paper examined weight loss together with valvular disease in fen-phen patients. [4]

A 1997 New England Journal of Medicine report from the Mayo Clinic linked fen-phen to mitral valve dysfunction; about 30 percent of long-term users (up to 24 months) had abnormal echocardiograms, though they had no symptoms, versus under 3 percent for use of three months or less. [1] A later study found that the severity of valve disease among affected patients was related to fenfluramine dose. [5]

Pharmacology research found that fenfluramine's metabolite stimulates serotonin 5-HT2B receptors on heart valves, producing changes histologically like those of carcinoid disease or ergot-drug exposure. [6][7]

The drugs were linked to pulmonary hypertension, a rare and often fatal lung condition. A 1999 review traced the link back to the earlier appetite suppressant aminorex, which was associated with an epidemic of the disease in Europe. [1][8]

Rat studies of phentermine and fenfluramine given separately and as a mixture described their distinct neurochemical effects. [9] Receptorome screening research identified 5-HT2B activation as the likely target responsible for the valve side effects. [10]

The US regulatory history of appetite suppressants, reviewed in the Annals of Internal Medicine, has swung between approving amphetamine-like drugs and restricting them as risks emerged. [3] Dexfenfluramine was approved in 1996 without a black box warning, despite an FDA medical officer's objections. [1] After the Mayo report, the FDA asked for withdrawal in September 1997. [1]

More than 50,000 product liability lawsuits were filed. [1] Wikipedia gives differing estimates of total liability and reports that Wyeth set aside $21.1 billion and offered settlements of $5,000 to $200,000. [1]
Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine were withdrawn from the US market in 1997. [1] Phentermine alone remained available as a prescription drug.
Preclinical studies in animals have tested fenfluramine plus phentermine and fluoxetine plus phentermine on cocaine self-administration. [11]

The principal human data are the 1984 Rochester trial of the combination, the 1997 Mayo Clinic echocardiographic findings, and later studies of weight loss and valve disease in people who had taken it. [1][4][5] A study of dose-effect among patients with valvulopathy found that fenfluramine dose was related to severity. [5]
